slides.label: Ray Tracing
slides.notes: Open by framing ray tracing as an image-order contract rather than a visual trick. Every pixel asks a geometric question, the scene answers with the nearest valid surface hit, and shading turns that record into color. The source span and notebook both emphasize inspectable data moving through this pipeline.

slides.label: The Three Verbs
slides.notes: Use the diagram as a control-flow map for the chapter. Ray generation, intersection, and shading are not independent black boxes; the interval chosen for a ray affects the closest hit, the hit record supplies shading data, and the shader may launch more rays with new intervals.

slides.label: Image Order Versus Object Order
slides.notes: Contrast the two loop nests without making one sound universally superior. Image-order rendering asks what each pixel sees, which makes shadows and mirror queries natural. Object-order rendering asks where each object lands on the image, which becomes central later in the pipeline chapters.

slides.label: Perspective Starts With A Camera Frame
slides.notes: Slow down on the camera basis because many ray-tracing bugs begin here. The eye point is not enough; students need the rightward, upward, and backward directions to be orthonormal and consistently oriented. Once that frame is trusted, pixel coordinates become points on a view window.

slides.label: Pixel Centers Become Window Coordinates
slides.notes: The half-pixel offset is small enough to look harmless and important enough to shift every sample. Ask learners to compare the blue center samples with the amber corner samples. The equation is less about algebra than about committing to a precise sampling convention before any ray is traced.

slides.label: A Ray Carries An Active Interval
slides.notes: Treat the interval as part of the ray query, not as an afterthought. Negative parameters are behind the eye, very small positive parameters can be numerical self-hits, and the upper endpoint changes when we already know a nearer surface. This convention will unify primary, shadow, and reflection rays.

slides.label: Sphere Intersections Are Quadratic Tests
slides.notes: Present the sphere case as the cleanest example of substituting a parametric ray into an implicit surface. The discriminant tells the geometry before any square root is interpreted. Then the interval test decides which root, if any, is visible to the current ray query.

slides.label: Triangle Hits Need Barycentric Discipline
slides.notes: A plane hit is not automatically a triangle hit. The barycentric coordinates are the bookkeeping that decide whether the ray crosses the filled triangle or only its supporting plane. Emphasize that the same solve returns depth along the ray and coordinates on the surface.

slides.label: Hit Records Are The Interface Boundary
slides.notes: Use this slide to move from equations into software architecture. Surfaces should not just answer yes or no; they should return the parameter, point data, normal, material reference, and surface identity needed by later stages. That interface makes spheres, triangles, groups, and acceleration structures interchangeable.

slides.label: Closest Hit Shrinks The Search
slides.notes: The active interval becomes a correctness device in a group intersection. Whenever a nearer hit is found, later tests are only allowed to report something closer. That rule prevents a far object from overwriting the visible surface and also avoids wasting work on intersections that cannot matter.

slides.label: Shading Begins With Four Vectors
slides.notes: After intersection, shading is no longer mysterious illumination; it is geometry at one point. The point, normal, light direction, and view direction determine the inputs to the material rule. Make students check normalization here, because nonunit vectors silently corrupt dot products and highlight widths.

slides.label: Lights And Materials Split Responsibilities
slides.notes: Explain the design choice as a way to keep the renderer extensible. A light knows where illumination comes from and a material knows how the surface responds to directions. Adding contributions across lights is simple, but the split keeps future area lights, textures, and better reflectance models from tangling the whole shader.

slides.label: Shadow Rays Ask A Visibility Question
slides.notes: A shadow ray is just another intersection query with a carefully chosen segment. The lower bound is positive so the ray does not immediately rediscover the surface it starts from, and the upper bound reaches the light only for point lights. The result is a binary visibility gate for that light contribution.

slides.label: Mirror Reflection Reuses The Same Query
slides.notes: Mirror reflection is powerful because it adds no new intersection machinery. Reflect the incoming direction about the normal, launch a secondary ray with an epsilon start, and multiply the returned color by a mirror coefficient. The depth counter is the explicit engineering guard against infinite bouncing.

slides.label: Numerical Guardrails
slides.notes: Collect the chapter hazards into a practical debugging checklist. A plausible image can still hide a flipped camera frame, unordered quadratic roots, a triangle plane false positive, or shadow acne. The notebook checks are valuable because they attach each visual artifact to a small invariant.

slides.label: Mini Renderer Laboratory
slides.notes: Connect the lecture back to the notebook lab without embedding its generated images. The experiment is intentionally small so every rendered feature can be traced to a data record: closest hit for visibility, normals for direct lighting, blockers for shadows, and recursive rays for reflective contributions.

slides.label: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by naming the transferable ideas. Ray tracing is easy to state because the outer loop is just over pixels, but reliable implementations depend on exact camera sampling, interval-aware intersections, rich hit records, and secondary rays with numerical offsets and termination rules.
